$comment: What this study says about this animal. `record` names the homology group a row has been assigned to; null means nobody has assigned it yet, and `blockedBy` says what is missing. `status` mirrors data/remine-status.json: `scaffolded` means these rows came out of the old storage and NOBODY HAS CHECKED THEM AGAINST THE PAPER.

observations.name: Adductor mandibulae
observations.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 1. **This lizard has eleven mandibular muscles against a human's eight**, which is the count that makes their point: the mammalian head is not the elaborated end of the series. The A2-PVM bundle here is the one they derive the mammalian tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini from. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

observations.name: Depressor mandibulae
observations.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 2. One undivided muscle. **This lizard has three hyoid muscles in total** — this one, the cervicomandibularis and the interhyoideus — against a platypus's twelve and a human's twenty-seven. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

observations.name: Dorsal mandibular muscles
observations.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 1, dorsal mandibular block. Three muscles here, against none in any of the five mammals they examined. Their caption is careful about the levator bulbi: the overall analysis makes the urodele one a dorsal mandibular muscle, **but they cannot completely rule out that it derives from the adductor mandibulae**, and it is drawn with a grey arrow on that reading rather than a black one. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

observations.name: Geniohyoid and rectus cervicis groups
observations.divisionNote: Diogo et al. sort the series into Edgeworth's two groups — 'geniohyoideus' and 'rectus cervicis'. The first three parts here are the geniohyoideus group, the last two the rectus cervicis group.
observations.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 4. **No well-developed independent intrinsic tongue muscles are counted for any taxon in this table** — the counts in its header all read 'not in. to.' — but amniotes have them and extant amphibians such as salamanders do not (Piatt 1938, Saban 1968, 1971). Edgeworth (1935) reads the hyoglossus of lizards such as *Timon* as corresponding to part of the coracomandibularis of amphibians and sarcopterygian fish. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

observations.name: Hyobranchialis and 'ceratohyoideus'
observations.divisionNote: Diogo et al. read both as a subdivision of the subarcualis rectus I. They quote the lizard 'ceratohyoideus' because it is not the mammalian muscle of that name, and they rename the other muscle hyobranchialis rather than branchiohyoideus because it is not homologous with the salamander hyoid muscle so called.
observations.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 3. **Adult lizards lack the branchial muscles sensu stricto as a group** — every one of them except these two. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

observations.name: Interhyoideus
observations.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 2. One muscle. **This is the row the whole facial musculature comes out of**: in their scheme a fan of arrows runs from this single lizard muscle to the platypus's interhyoideus profundus, sphincter colli superficialis, cervicalis transversa, orbicularis oculi, buccinatorius, naso-labialis and orbicularis oris, and on into the therian face. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

observations.name: Intermandibularis posterior and intermandibularis anterior
observations.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 1. Both divisions present under their plain names — the arrangement the mammalian rows have to be read against. **No attachments are scored: this source is a scheme of correspondences and describes none.**
